While diffusion models generate high-fidelity video clips, transforming them into coherent storytelling
engines remains challenging.
Current agentic pipelines automate this via chained modules but
suffer from semantic drift and cascading failures due to independent, handcrafted prompting. We
present Co-Director, a hierarchical multi-agent framework formalizing video storytelling as a global
optimization problem. To ensure semantic coherence, we introduce hierarchical parameterization:
a multi-armed bandit globally identifies promising creative directions, while a local multimodal
self-refinement loop mitigates identity drift and ensures sequence-level consistency. This balances the
exploration of novel narrative strategies with the exploitation of effective creative configurations. For
evaluation, we introduce GenAd-Bench, a 400-scenario dataset of fictional products for personalized
advertising. Experiments demonstrate that Co-Director significantly outperforms state-of-the-art
baselines, offering a principled approach that seamlessly generalizes to broader cinematic narratives.

1. Introduction
Generative video storytelling aims to transform abstract ideas—such as a simple tagline and sparse
reference visuals—into cohesive video narratives, like a fully realized short film. It has diverse
applications, ranging from democratizing high-end content creation (Divya and Mirza, 2024) to
automating filmmaking (Zhang et al., 2025) and digital advertising (Baek, 2023). Realizing this
potential requires jointly optimizing multiple objectives: narrative coherence, visual consistency,
and mise-en-scène—the visual language dictating how camera angles, color palettes, and metaphors
deliver the intended message (Zettl, 1973).
Recent advancements in video diffusion demonstrate remarkable high-fidelity generation. High-
profile collaborations, such as Google DeepMind’s work with Darren Aronofsky on Ancestra (Aronofsky
and McNitt, 2025) and On This Day... 1776 (Aronofsky, 2026), showcase the artistic ceiling when
backed by a 200-person creative team. While representing the pinnacle of human-AI collaboration,
such resources remain out of reach for independent creators. Without them, individuals must
manually bridge the gap between LLM scripting and fragmented generative models, correcting for
the consistency errors and identity drift inherent in current architectures (Elmoghany et al., 2025).
To mitigate this, the community has pivoted toward agentic pipelines where LLMs orchestrate
the multi-step generative process (Huang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2025; Wei et al.,
2025; Wu et al., 2025b). However, these systems remain susceptible to “cascading failures,” where
early errors propagate and break long-horizon consistency (Zhou et al., 2024). This reflects the
classical credit assignment problem (Minsky, 1961), as terminal failures are difficult to trace back to
specific prompts. Furthermore, existing systems rely on static, handcrafted prompt templates lacking

a unified creative vision. Without a mechanism to map script-level changes to downstream generation,
the resulting visual output often feels disjointed. Crucially, these approaches fail to capture the
serendipity essential to creative production. Human directors often explore counter-intuitive ideas to
find “creative gold.” Static, chained pipelines are fundamentally ill-equipped for such exploration,
remaining anchored to fixed templates unable to adapt to the non-linear nature of creative success.
In this work, we present Co-Director, a multi-agent framework for automating video storytelling.
To the best of our knowledge, Co-Director is the first system to formalize generative storytelling
as a global optimization problem. Unlike prior agentic pipelines that rely on linear, "waterfall" chains
prone to semantic drift, we introduce a hierarchical parameterization strategy steered by Multi-Armed
Bandit (MAB) (Bubeck and Cesa-Bianchi, 2012). Rather than relying on fixed prompt templates,
Co-Director utilizes MAB to sample abstract creative trajectories and dynamically injects these into
the system prompts of sub-agents. This top-down steering ensures that all-agents—from script-writing
to video generation—are orthogonally aligned toward a unified creative intent. This formulation
formalizes the creative process as a search for the optimal balance between exploration—venturing into
novel, unconventional narrative territories—and exploitation—refining historically effective stylistic
configurations. This allows Co-Director to move beyond simple self-correction toward a principled
exploration of the creative latent space, identifying the configuration that optimally balances visual
fidelity with narrative effectiveness (Escalas, 2004).
Furthermore, we argue that evaluating video storytelling requires a shift from open-ended cin-
ematic metrics towards rigorous, constraint-driven frameworks. We use digital advertising as our
demonstration scenario because it demands both sophisticated storytelling (much like short cinematic
film) and strict adherence to objective requirements: asset preservation, audience alignment, and
value proposition communication (Teixeira et al., 2012). To this end, we introduce GenAd-Bench,
a dataset of 400 scenarios across 200 fictional products. By utilizing fictional entities, we respect
copyright constraints while preventing models from defaulting to memorized training priors. We
provide a multimodal LLM (MLLM)-based evaluation suite covering Visual Asset Fidelity, Demographic
Alignment, Visual Quality, and Marketing Appeal—anchored in the AIDA hierarchy (Barry and Howard,
1990; Strong, 1925).
Our primary contributions are summarized as follows:
• We propose Co-Director, a multi-agent architecture for video storytelling that achieves global
coherence by integrating multi-armed bandit optimization with a local, MLLM feedback-driven
refinement loop.
• We introduce the hierarchical parameterization of creative intent, enabling the consistent propa-
gation of visual and narrative styles across discrete generative sub-agents.
• We present GenAd-Bench to rigorously evaluate generative video storytelling across 400
scenarios, eliminating memorization bias via the use of fictional brand assets.
• We demonstrate our approach significantly outperforming existing foundation models and agentic
baselines in asset preservation, contextual alignment, and visual quality.
• We open-source our implementation of Co-Director and the GenAd-Bench dataset to
facilitate future research in generative video storytelling.

Agentic Frameworks for Video Storytelling
To bridge the gap between clip generation and
narrative production, recent multi-agent systems utilize LLMs to decompose scripts into shot lists and
prompts (Lin et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025b), targeting domains like personalized vlogs (Hou et al.,
2025), music videos (Tang et al., 2025), and short films (Mu et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2025; Xiao et al.,
2025; Zhao et al., 2024). However, these “waterfall” pipelines are susceptible to cascading errors.
While frameworks like AniMaker (Shi et al., 2025) and MAViS (Wang et al., 2026) incorporate local
consistency checks, they struggle with global credit assignment (Minsky, 1961) across the agentic
stack. To resolve this, Co-Director moves beyond the local-refinement paradigm by introducing a
Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) formulation (Bubeck and Cesa-Bianchi, 2012; Lai and Robbins, 1985) to
perform a principled exploration-exploitation of the creative latent space. This global, hierarchical
parameterization resolves the “semantic collisions” between sub-agents that plague current pipelines,
preventing identity drift and ensuring horizontal cohesiveness.
Benchmarks for Video Storytelling
As generative capabilities evolve, evaluation methodologies
must adapt to measure higher-order reasoning. Generic video benchmarks (Huang et al., 2024; Sun
et al., 2025) focus on prompt alignment and broad aesthetics, lacking the visual and narrative qualities
demanded by professional workflows. Furthermore, even recent narrative-focused benchmarks, such
as MovieBench (Wu et al., 2025a) and ViStoryBench (Zhuang et al., 2025), strictly evaluate isolated
generative sub-tasks using meticulously pre-defined scripts. Consequently, current literature lacks
evaluations for true end-to-end storytelling: the complex process of autonomously transforming a
simple, abstract idea into a cohesive video narrative. Our work addresses this gap by introducing
GenAd-Bench designed specifically for end-to-end generative workflows.

3. Approach
3.1. Hierarchical Multi-Agent Architecture
We formulate Co-Director as a hierarchical multi-agent system orchestrating generative video
workflows. While the framework is domain-agnostic, we instantiate it to solve video advertising, which
comes with strict narrative and visual constraints.
Orchestrator Agent (Φ𝑜𝑟𝑐ℎ)
This agent manages the global state and execution flow of all sub-agents.
Before downstream generation, it performs multimodal data ingestion: 1) parsing the user prompt
𝑝𝑢𝑠𝑒𝑟into structured constraints ˆ𝑝𝑢𝑠𝑒𝑟(brand, product, and demographics (Baardman et al., 2021)); 2)
annotating reference visuals I𝑟𝑒𝑓with captions and semantic roles (e.g., product, logo, protagonist),
yielding ˆI𝑟𝑒𝑓. Post-initialization, Φ𝑜𝑟𝑐ℎdrives a global optimization loop for 𝑇iterations. At iteration 𝑡,
it interfaces with a multi-armed bandit (Section 3.3) to sample a creative configuration 𝜃(𝑡), forming
a global conditioning context Θ(𝑡) = (ˆ𝑝𝑢𝑠𝑒𝑟, ˆI𝑟𝑒𝑓, 𝜃(𝑡)),1 which is then propagated downstream.
Pre-Production Agent (Φ𝑝𝑟𝑒)
This agent transforms the structured constraints Θ into a descriptive
storyboard S through four sequential modules:
• Creative Brief (B): Acting as the “deep research” phase, this module performs contextual enrich-
ment, expanding product/demographic constraints within ˆ𝑝𝑢𝑠𝑒𝑟into localized cultural resonance
and environmental context. This becomes a creative brief B.
• Storyline (L): Conditioned on B and 𝜃, this module constructs the storyline L that acts as a
scene-by-scene script establishing plot, character actions, pacing, and transitions.
• Visual Assets (V): This module generates visual assets V for entities in L (e.g., characters,
props, environments) only if they are absent from the reference visuals ˆI𝑟𝑒𝑓∈Θ. For characters, it
synthesizes context-aligned wardrobes dictated by L, compositing the base character and garments
into multi-angle reference collages.
• Storyboard (S): Expands L into a storyboard S = {𝑠0, . . . , 𝑠𝑁−1} modulated by 𝜃. Each scene
𝑠𝑖∈S defines semantic descriptors (actions, environment), camera kinematics (scale, movements),
temporal constraints, and entity presence flags linked to V. It also formulates global audio directives
(voiceover, tempo, mood), inspired by consumer psychology literature (Alpert and Alpert, 1990;
Gorn, 1982).

3.2. Local Optimization via Agentic Self-Refinement
In sequential generative pipelines, early errors propagate and amplify downstream. To prevent this,
Co-Director implements feedback descent (Lee et al., 2025; Yuksekgonul et al., 2024) to self-refine
intermediate artifacts. LLMs and MLLMs iteratively evaluate and refine artifacts based on textual
feedback. This loop terminates upon reaching a score threshold or iteration budget, returning the
best attempt. We apply this local optimization to storyline L and keyframes K, reserving final video
evaluation for a global reward signal (Section 3.3)
Storyline
Before Φ𝑝𝑟𝑒generates storyboard S, an LLM assesses storyline L on hook quality, narrative
cohesion, product integration, emotional engagement, and prompt adherence. It outputs a score with
textual feedback and rewrites the prompt to emphasize areas needing improvement. If the score falls
below threshold 𝜏L, the agent regenerates L using this revised prompt, ensuring a coherent narrative
foundation before expansion into S.
Keyframe
An MLLM evaluates the keyframe sequence K = {𝑘0, . . . , 𝑘𝑁−1} jointly rather than
individually. This joint contextualization evaluates sequence-level consistency for character and
product identities, alongside environmental continuity. Comparing K against ˆ𝑝𝑢𝑠𝑒𝑟and V, it scores
visual consistency, narrative flow, product appeal, and prompt adherence. If the aggregate score
falls below threshold 𝜏K, the MLLM isolates issues and indexes problematic keyframes in K. It then
provides actionable feedback and refined prompts, allowing Φ 𝑓𝑟𝑎𝑚𝑒to selectively regenerate flagged
keyframes while preserving accepted ones.
3.3. Global Optimization via Multi-Armed Bandits
Because the chained pipeline is non-differentiable, standard gradient updates cannot achieve end-to-
end optimization. Instead, Co-Director uses hierarchical parameterization, treating the pipeline as a
black box steered by centralized parameters governing global creative directions. We formulate tuning
these parameters as a Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problem (Bubeck and Cesa-Bianchi, 2012; Lai and
Robbins, 1985). Operating at this top level, rather than tuning individual prompts independently,
ensures semantic coherence across sub-agents while balancing the exploration of novel strategies
with the exploitation of proven configurations.
MAB Preliminaries
In a standard MAB framework, an agent iteratively selects an action (an “arm”),
observes a reward, and updates its policy to maximize long-term payout. The central challenge is the
exploration-exploitation tradeoff: balancing testing untried arms for potentially higher rewards against
exploiting the best-known option. In Co-Director, a single “pull” corresponds to a full pipeline
execution, the “arms” are creative directions 𝜃, and the “reward” is the terminal video evaluation
score.

Hierarchical Parameterization
We define the action space (the “arms”) over three orthogonal axes
of video production grounded in marketing and media theory. The creative direction 𝜃is a tuple
comprising three categorical variables: 𝜃= (𝜃𝑐𝑠, 𝜃𝑛𝑚, 𝜃𝑎𝑎).
• Creative Strategy (𝜃𝑐𝑠): This controls what the ad is fundamentally trying to communicate (Laskey
et al., 1989). The bandit selects among an Informational strategy (focusing on functional utility),
a Transformational strategy (driving psychological and lifestyle appeal), or a Comparative strategy
(positioning against a known standard or competitor).
• Narrative Mode (𝜃𝑛𝑚): This controls how the strategy is delivered over time (Escalas, 2004). The
bandit selects among an Analytical mode (an argument-based delivery without a story arc), a
Vignette mode (atmospheric slices-of-life prioritizing mood over plot), or a Narrative Drama mode
(a character-driven sequence of conflict and resolution).
• Aesthetic Archetype (𝜃𝑎𝑎): This controls the sensory realization of the video (Zettl, 1973) via four
configurations: Clarity/Energy (high-key lighting, fast-cut motion, high-tempo audio); Cinematic
Premium (chiaroscuro lighting, slow reflective camera work, orchestral audio); Minimalist Focus
(bright backgrounds, micro-movements, ASMR-style foley); and Kinetic Grit (low-key lighting,
handheld/FPV drone motion, electronic synth audio).
At execution step 𝑡, the MAB selects an arm combination 𝜃(𝑡). While downstream LLMs can interpret
these creative parameters, independent interpretation risks semantic drift. To ensure coherence,
orchestrator Φ𝑜𝑟𝑐ℎcentrally synthesizes 𝜃(𝑡) into agent-specific instructions, dynamically injecting
them into placeholders within the agents’ system prompts.
Reward
To evaluate 𝜃(𝑡), Co-Director uses an MLLM evaluator processing the final video 𝐹(𝑡)
alongside 𝑝𝑢𝑠𝑒𝑟and I𝑟𝑒𝑓to yield two metrics (full prompt in Appendix K). First, an aggregate quality
score (temporal coherence, visual quality, consistency) selects the best video across 𝑇executions.
Second, it computes dimension-specific strategic efficacy scores crucial for MAB optimization. This
decouples execution from strategy, assessing if the creative direction was effective independent of
downstream diffusion artifacts. This yields a factored reward signal 𝑅(𝑡) = (𝑟𝑐𝑠, 𝑟𝑛𝑚, 𝑟𝑎𝑎) ∈[0, 100]3 to
update the bandit’s policy.
Optimization Policy and Warm Start
Co-Director models the search using the Upper Confidence
Bound (UCB1) algorithm (Auer et al., 2002), which uses the disentangled scalars from 𝑅(𝑡) to
independently update the expected value of each selected arm. By decoupling the reward updates,
the MAB analytically bypasses the credit assignment problem (Minsky, 1961), isolating exactly which
creative strategies drove the video’s success or failure. Furthermore, because unguided exploration is
prohibitively expensive in video generation, we introduce an LLM-driven warm start. Prior to the first
execution, an LLM analyzes the user’s demographic and product domain to initialize the expected
values of the arms, safely biasing early exploration toward theoretically sound configurations.
4. GenAd-Bench: Evaluating Generative Video Advertising
To construct GenAd-Bench, we developed a human-in-the-loop pipeline using Gemini 3 Pro (Google,
2026b) for text synthesis and Nano Banana Pro (Google, 2026c) for visual assets. We generated 50
fictional brands with four products each, spanning consumer goods to industrial equipment. For each
product, we authored two contrasting demographics—stereotypical and unconventional—yielding
400 unique scenarios defined by a six-point prompt (brand, product, gender, age, location, interest).
Accompanying visual assets (logos, product references) were generated and manually verified (15%
required regeneration) to ensure uniqueness and prevent visual memorization or copyright conflicts.
The resulting benchmark enforces strict targeting constraints and multimodal conditioning,

requiring models to synthesize textual demographic intent with specific reference imagery. By
evaluating paired scenarios across a global geographic distribution, GenAd-Bench explicitly
tests conceptual flexibility and exposure to ingrained biases. Furthermore, by utilizing fictional
entities, the benchmark prevents models from defaulting to memorized training priors, ensuring that
performance is a measure of reasoning rather than retrieval. We partition the data into half (200
scenarios each) for hillclimbing and validation.
We use Gemini 3 Pro (Google, 2026b) as an MLLM-as-a-Judge to evaluate generated videos; see
Appendix L for the rubric prompts. The MLLM simultaneously processes visual frames and the audio
track to score four dimensions (0–100):
• Visual Asset Fidelity (VAF): Measures faithfulness to user-provided logos and products. The MLLM
assesses visual-semantic similarity, ensuring core identity preservation across complex camera
angles, occlusions, and dynamic lighting.
• Demographic Alignment (DA): Assesses targeting success across four variables (Gender, Age,
Location, Interest). The MLLM penalizes generic aesthetics while rewarding tailored casting,
localized environmental context, and narrative tone.
• Marketing Appeal (MA): Evaluates advertisement persuasiveness via the AIDA hierarchy (Barry
and Howard, 1990; Strong, 1925) and engagement theory (Teixeira et al., 2012). It scores visual
hooks, value proposition clarity, and emotional resonance.
• Visual Quality (VQ): A prompt-agnostic metric scanning for diffusion artifacts, object morphing,
and temporal flickering. It ensures videos meet broadcast viability by penalizing unnatural motion
or violations of basic physical laws.
While utilizing an MLLM for evaluation raises potential bias concerns, we benchmark these metrics
against a human study (Section 5.2). We find that the MLLM serves as a reliable proxy, showing
alignment that approaches the human-human agreement ceiling.
5. Experiments
We evaluate Co-Director on GenAd-Bench against state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating
its superior storytelling capabilities, followed by ablation studies validating the necessity of local
self-refinement and global MAB optimization.
Implementation Details
We instantiate Co-Director with Gemini 3 Pro (Google, 2026b), Nano
Banana Pro (Google, 2026c), Veo 3.1 (Google, 2026d), Gemini 2.5 Pro TTS (Google, 2026a), and
Lyria 2 (Google, 2025). MAB optimization is set to 𝑇= 4 iterations (see App. F for search efficiency
trade-offs), and local refinement is capped at 3 retries. Final videos feature 4 shots totaling 12
seconds.
Baselines
We evaluate Co-Director against monolithic models, commercial platforms, and multi-
agent frameworks, listed in Table 1. To isolate architectural efficacy, we compare against analogous
agentic pipelines AniMaker and MovieAgent using the same underlying models. Since these require

Finally, we compare Co-Director against a Base Agentic Pipeline (no optimizations) and a
Random Search Baseline (𝑇= 4) that samples the creative space without MAB or warm-up. Baseline
details are in Appendix E.

5.1. Main Results
As reported in Table 1, Co-Director achieves the highest average performance (81.4). We include
specialized commercial platforms (Creatify, HeyGen) to establish the current industry baseline; their
reliance on "talking head" avatar synthesis with static overlays fundamentally limits their performance
on complex narratives, highlighting the necessity of Co-Director’s dynamic storytelling. Crucially,
the performance gap between Co-Director and prior agentic baselines (AniMaker, MovieAgent)
stems strictly from agentic architectural differences. By utilizing the same LLM (Gemini 3 Pro) to
generate their requisite input scripts, we ensured a highly competitive and equitable starting point.
Furthermore, self-refinement (Section 3.2) and MAB optimization (Section 3.3) drive Co-Director’s

5.3. Ablation Studies
MAB Logic
We compare our MAB search logic (1) against two variants. Reverting to a cold start (2)
degrades performance, as lacking strong initialization produces higher-variance trajectories during
early exploration. Crucially, collapsing the multi-dimensional arm-specific reward into a single scalar
(3)—using the holistic score meant for final video selection—reduces VAF by 5.0 points. This validates
our factored reward design. By leveraging the MLLM evaluator to decouple the overall video score
from arm-specific rewards, the MAB isolates the exact parameters driving success (see App. K).
Self-Refinement Loops
Removing Storyline Refinement (4) primarily penalizes semantic metrics
like MA and DA, validating its impact on narrative coherence. Removing Keyframe Refinement (5)
causes a steep 9.8-point VAF drop, confirming its vital role in preserving product visual identity.
Stripping all local refinement and global optimization yields a “barebones” single-pass baseline (8)
(67.2 Avg.). Our complete architecture outperforms this linear performance floor by a relative 17.6%.

6. Conclusion
We present Co-Director, a hierarchical multi-agent framework that formulates video storytelling
as a global optimization problem. By navigating a creative latent space via MAB-driven steering, our

C. Evaluation on General Video Storytelling
In the main paper, we chose video advertising as our main demonstration scenario because it highlights
a novel aspect of our framework: the ability to generate a full video narrative from a single, high-
level idea, rather than needing a detailed, scene-by-scene script. Existing agentic systems, such
as AniMaker (Shi et al., 2025) and MovieAgent (Wu et al., 2025b), require structured, scene-by-
scene scripts provided a priori. In contrast, our framework synthesizes full cohesive narratives from
a brief tagline (e.g., our six-point prompt). While MAViS (Wang et al., 2026) attempts a similar
idea-to-video pipeline, their evaluation relies on a closed set of 10 custom prompts, precluding
reproducible comparison. This underscores the critical importance of our proposed GenAd-Bench.
Existing visual narrative datasets, such as MovieBench (Wu et al., 2025a) and ViStoryBench (Zhuang
et al., 2025), evaluate isolated generative steps (e.g., text-to-image or image-to-video synthesis)
rather than the complete video storytelling pipeline. GenAd-Bench fills this void by providing
a rigorous, reproducible standard for evaluating the entire trajectory of video storytelling—from
abstract conceptualization to final rendered output.
Despite the architectural mismatch between our end-to-end framework and traditional staged
benchmarks, we evaluate Co-Director on ViStoryBench-Lite (Zhuang et al., 2025) to demonstrate
its generality across domains. Because ViStoryBench evaluates storyboard generation—providing
strict shot-by-shot scripts and character reference images as inputs, and expecting static image outputs
rather than video—we ablate our pipeline accordingly. Specifically, we bypass our script generation and
video synthesis modules, isolating and deploying only the Keyframe Agent, the local self-refinement
loop, and the global MAB-steered optimization. This allows us to prove that Co-Director’s core
consistency and creative direction mechanisms remain highly effective even when constrained to rigid,
pre-defined narrative structures. To ensure a rigorous evaluation, we deliberately select agentic video
generation pipelines from the official ViStoryBench leaderboard as our baselines, as their modular
architectures provide the most direct and equitable comparison to our own.

D.2. Taxonomy and Distribution Statistics
GenAd-Bench contains 400 evaluation scenarios distributed across a diverse range of industries
and global contexts.
Macro-Category Distribution
The dataset challenges models to render various physical proper-
ties, including reflective metals (Jewelry), transparent liquids (Perfumes), and complex dynamics

High-frequency categories such as Home Goods (24), Food (20), Fashion (20), and Tech (20), test

Demographic and Geographic Parity
To ensure the multi-armed bandit optimization does not

cultural and environmental alignment beyond traditional Western-centric backdrops; the scenarios are
grounded in 183 uniquely prompted global locations. While the dataset spans all six major continents,
it deliberately concentrates on the two most diverse global consumer markets: Europe (158 scenarios)
and Asia (108 scenarios). Within these clusters, geographic representation remains highly granular.
The European scenarios span from primary Western hubs (e.g., France, UK, Germany) to Nordic and
Eastern European locales, while the Asian distribution covers major East Asian centers (Japan, China,
South Korea) alongside robust representation across Southeast Asia, India, and the Middle East.

F. Extended Discussion on MAB Optimization Efficiency
While standard multi-armed bandit (MAB) formulations often analyze asymptotic convergence over
thousands of iterations, video generation imposes extreme computational and financial constraints. An
exhaustive grid search of our defined creative action space (𝜃𝑐𝑠× 𝜃𝑛𝑚× 𝜃𝑎𝑎) would require 36 discrete,
end-to-end video generation pipelines per prompt. While this brute-force approach guarantees finding
the global optimum, it renders the system entirely unscalable and defeats the purpose of an accessible
agentic framework.
Therefore, the goal of our MAB formulation is not infinite-horizon exploration, but rather sample
efficiency under resource constraints. We achieve this through two mechanisms:
1. Factored Rewards: By utilizing a factored reward signal 𝑅= (𝑟𝑐𝑠, 𝑟𝑛𝑚, 𝑟𝑎𝑎), a single execution
step 𝑡simultaneously updates the expected values across all three independent creative axes.
The system is not searching 36 distinct paths, but rather evaluating 10 independent parameters.
2. LLM-Driven Warm Start: We initialize the expected values using an LLM, safely biasing
early exploration toward theoretically sound configurations and pruning the vast majority of
sub-optimal combinations before iteration even begins.
Consequently, as demonstrated in our empirical results (Fig. 2), an iteration budget of 𝑇= 4 is
sufficient for the MAB to rapidly converge on a highly effective creative configuration. This approach
clearly outperforms Random Search, capturing the benefits of a global search without incurring the
computational overhead of exhaustive sampling.

G.1. Horizontal Directing through Hierarchical Parameterization
Co-Director achieves global coherence through horizontal directing—the process of synthesizing
disparate creative parameters into a unified, high-level vision. Rather than passing raw categorical
arms as static strings, the Orchestrator Agent (Φ𝑜𝑟𝑐ℎ) generates a top-down creative direction that
is decomposed into agent-specific technical directives. These directives are then routed to their
respective sub-agents via dynamic prompt injection; specifically, the synthesized creative direction
is injected into the system prompt of each agent. This ensures that the Storyline, Keyframe, and
Video instructions are orthogonally aligned toward a single strategic goal, preventing semantic drift
by grounding each agent’s execution in a centralized creative intent.
